# PrototypeFramework — the agent contract for a consuming SKU

**Source:** `com.classicspins.prototype-framework` · this file ships inside the package and is
synced into your repo. **Do not edit it here or in your repo** — edit it in the framework repo at
`Packages/com.classicspins.prototype-framework/Documentation~/agent/AGENTS.framework.md`, then
re-sync. A local edit is overwritten by the next sync and fails `agentdocs --check` until then.

This is the **rules half** of the pack. The shape half is `architecture-map.md`; the procedures
are in `recipes/`; the type lookup is `framework-api.index.json`.

---

## §0 — The five things that get a change rejected at review

Before anything else, these are the failure modes that actually happen:

1. **You edited framework code from inside the SKU.** See §5 — it is always wrong, and the
   mechanism that makes it wrong is different for each dev-link mode.
2. **You wrote a command-style event** (`ShowDialogEvent`, `PlaySfxEvent`). See rule #1.
3. **Your View branched on game state.** See §3, the "why" test.
4. **You put a script where no assembly claims it.** A `.cs` with no ancestor `.asmdef`/`.asmref`
   compiles into the predefined `Assembly-CSharp`, which auto-references everything — so it builds
   green while sitting outside the AD-1 boundary. Every SKU script belongs under a layer folder;
   `Framework/Doctor` check 15 names the ones that do not.
5. **You made a spine change without routing it.** See §6 — a new assembly, reference edge,
   RenderLayer, boot node, event type, or an edit to a shipped migrator is not a local decision.

## §1 — The 17 rules

The canonical wording is Vietnamese and is reproduced **verbatim** — do not translate, reword, or
"clean up" the table. The English gloss is a convenience; **when the gloss and the verbatim text
seem to differ, the verbatim rule wins.**

| # | Rule (verbatim) | English gloss | How it is enforced |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Event là **sự thật quá khứ**, không phải mệnh lệnh — cấm event dạng lệnh (`ShowDialogEvent`, `PlaySfxEvent`); muốn ai làm gì thì gọi service của họ | Events are past-tense **facts**, not commands — command-style events are banned; to make something happen, call that owner's service. | Review. A `*Event` name in the imperative is the tell. |
| 2 | **Migrator đã ship là bất biến** — không sửa, chỉ append migrator + fixture mới | **A shipped migrator is immutable** — never edit it; only append a new migrator + new fixture. | Migration-fixture tests (`TestCategory=DataValidation`). Editing a shipped migrator reddens an old fixture. |
| 3 | Cấm `string.Split(',')` khi parse CSV — dùng parser RFC 4180 đúng nghĩa | Never `string.Split(',')` to parse CSV — use a proper RFC 4180 parser. | Review + the loc-CSV validation stage. |
| 4 | Không chuỗi literal nào đi vào `SetText` từ code game — text đi qua `LocKey` | No string literal reaches `SetText` from game code — all text goes through `LocKey`. | Review. Every user-visible string is a `LocKey` from the Master CSV. |
| 5 | Node boot chỉ được đụng service nó đã khai trong `Requires` | A boot node may only touch services it declared in its `Requires` capabilities. | `BootGraph.Validate()` + the race rule in §4. |
| 6 | Framework không tự đẩy node sang thread khác — việc nặng CPU node tự `UniTask.RunOnThreadPool` bên trong | The framework never moves a node off-thread for you — a CPU-heavy node self-hops via `UniTask.RunOnThreadPool` internally. | Review. The kernel awaits on the main thread by design. |
| 7 | Thêm RenderLayer phải trả lời được tiêu chí ba-điều-kiện; không trả lời được = dùng `sortingOrder` trong layer sẵn có | Adding a RenderLayer must satisfy the three-condition test; if it can't, use `sortingOrder` within an existing layer. | Spine change — route it (§6). Three conditions in `architecture-map.md` §5. |
| 8 | Hai phép thử View khi review: test "vì sao" + test gallery | Two View review tests: the "why" test + the gallery test. | Review — see §3. |
| 9 | Cấm poll input (`Input.GetTouch`, `OnMouse*`, `Touchscreen.current`) trong `Game.Views` — mọi pointer input qua EventSystem; ngoại lệ duy nhất là `IBackButtonRouter` | No input polling in `Game.Views` — all pointer input via EventSystem; the sole exception is `IBackButtonRouter`. | **CI grep** — `Tools/CI/greps.sh source` names `file:line`. |
| 10 | Controller không thấy tọa độ screen-space — View đổi sang đơn vị game (cell/reel index) trước khi phát event/gesture | A controller never sees screen-space coordinates — the View converts to game units before emitting an event/gesture. | Review. A `Vector2 screenPos` crossing into a controller is the tell. |
| 11 | WARN "rented leak" trong log CI là **lỗi phải sửa** (quên `Return`), không phải noise | A "rented leak" WARN in the CI log is **a bug to fix** (a missing `Return`), not noise. | **CI grep** — `greps.sh poolleak <log>` exits non-zero on `[PoolLeak]`. |
| 12 | Ranh giới vùng người/vùng máy: layout prefab uGUI (gồm cấu trúc layer text `TextProxy`), particle tune, bake, mixer routing — qua Unity-MCP, không sửa YAML/prefab thô | Human-zone / machine-zone boundary: uGUI prefab layout (incl. `TextProxy` text-layer stacks), particle tuning, bakes, mixer routing — go through Unity-MCP, never raw YAML/prefab edits. | Review — see §2. Raw YAML edits corrupt GUIDs/fileIDs. |
| 13 | Tạo scene/dialog/widget mới: sửa manifest → `Scaffold.Sync` — không tạo tay, không copy template thủ công | Creating a new scene/dialog/widget: edit the manifest → `Scaffold.Sync` — never hand-create, never manually copy a template. | `Scaffold.Sync --check` (four-legs drift gate) fails by name. |
| 14 | Model cấm `System.Random`/`UnityEngine.Random` — nhận `IRandom` qua constructor; seed đặt ở composition point, log seed để tái tạo phiên lỗi | Models must not use `System.Random`/`UnityEngine.Random` — inject `IRandom` via constructor; set the seed at the composition point and log it to reproduce failing sessions. | Review + the headless determinism tests. |
| 15 | Sim real-time: advance Model bằng **fixed dt** truyền qua param, cấm đọc `Time.*` trong Model; tick đi qua `GameplayTickDriver` (tick-entry duy nhất của scope), pause gate quyết tick chạy hay không | Real-time sim: advance the Model by a **fixed dt** passed as a parameter, never read `Time.*` inside a Model; ticks flow through `GameplayTickDriver` (the scope's sole tick entry); a pause gate decides whether the tick runs. | Review + a Model that reads `Time.*` cannot compile headlessly (Domain has `noEngineReferences`). |
| 16 | Parent quyết theo **từng object**, không quyết một lần cho cả feature: hỏi *neo vào đâu* trước — neo cạnh màn hình (HUD, score, top bar) ⇒ uGUI dưới `GetHost` của layer sở hữu nó (`Ui` cho screen furniture, `Popup` cho dialog, `Overlay` cho overlay hệ thống); neo trong thế giới ⇒ mới hỏi vẽ bằng gì (`Renderer` ⇒ `WorldRoot`, `Canvas` ⇒ `GetHost(id)`) | The parent is decided **per object**, never once for a whole feature: ask *what does it anchor to* first — anchored to a screen edge (HUD, score, top bar) ⇒ uGUI under the `GetHost` of the layer that owns it (`Ui` for screen furniture, `Popup` for dialogs, `Overlay` for system overlays); anchored in the world ⇒ only then ask how it draws (`Renderer` ⇒ `WorldRoot`, `Canvas` ⇒ `GetHost(id)`). | Review. The tell is one sentence in a plan fixing the draw path for a whole feature, or a HUD/score readout parented under `WorldRoot`. Procedure: [`recipes/add-world-object.md`](./recipes/add-world-object.md) · [`recipes/add-widget.md`](./recipes/add-widget.md). |
| 17 | Mọi bề mặt người chơi nhìn thấy phải ship ở trạng thái **hoàn thiện thị giác**, không phải wireframe: có art spec (`docs/art-direction.md`) ⇒ theo đúng spec; không có ⇒ agent **tự quyết** thẩm mỹ và ghi lại design token (bảng màu, thang khoảng cách, thang chữ) vào một file token duy nhất của SKU rồi index vào đó, cấm rải màu rời trong View; placeholder chỉ hợp lệ khi người **yêu cầu rõ ràng** | Every player-visible surface ships **visually finished**, not as a wireframe: if an art spec (`docs/art-direction.md`) exists, follow it; if none exists, the agent **decides** the aesthetics and records the design tokens (palette, spacing scale, type scale) in the SKU's single token file and indexes into it — never scatter loose colours through Views; a placeholder is legitimate only when the human **explicitly asked** for one. | Review + the finished-surface checklist in the `pf-visual-design` skill. The tell is a `Color`/hex literal in a View outside the token file, a rig-default background shipped as the game's, or a Verification section with no visual check on a feature that draws. |

## §2 — Human zone / machine zone

Some work is **isolated to the live Unity editor** and must be done **through Unity-MCP against a
running editor** — never by editing raw `.unity` / `.prefab` / `.asset` YAML. The live editor keeps
GUIDs and fileIDs consistent; raw edits corrupt them. This is the **human zone**:

- **uGUI prefab layout**, including building the `TextProxy` text-layer stacks (TMP layers, outline
  settings).
- **Particle tuning**, lighting/GI **bakes**, and audio **mixer routing**.
- **Master-Scene rig** work (cameras, canvases, EventSystem, render-layer hosts).

Agents operate in the **machine zone** — the key / CSV / code / manifest tier, edited directly and
diff-reviewable: `.cs`, `.asmdef`, `.json` (`package.json`, `manifest.json`, `*.json` manifests),
`.csv`, `.md`, `.sh`, `.yml`.

**When a task needs a prefab/scene/particle/mixer change, drive Unity-MCP. Do not hand-write YAML.**

> **The boundary is about mechanism, not authority.** It fixes *how* a prefab is edited — through the
> live editor, because raw YAML corrupts GUIDs — and says nothing about *who decides what the thing
> should look like*. Absent an artist's spec, the aesthetic call is **yours to make and to record**:
> see rule #17 and the `pf-visual-design` skill. Reading "human zone" as
> "visuals are not mine to decide" is what ships a working wireframe.

> Practical note: on macOS, Unity-MCP returns null while the Editor window is unfocused. If an MCP
> call hangs or returns nothing, that is the cause — ask the user to focus the Editor rather than
> retrying or falling back to raw YAML.

## §3 — The two View review tests

Every `Game.Views` View (a dumb `MonoBehaviour` at the prefab root) must pass **both** tests. They
operationalize "a View answers *how it looks*, a controller answers *what happens*":

1. **The "why" test.** If a View method needs to know *why* it was called, that decision belongs in
   the controller. A View must not decide "if the player can't afford it, disable the button" — the
   controller decides and calls `SetBuyEnabled(false)`. **A View never branches on game state.**
2. **The gallery test.** Every View method must be callable in **any order**, in a scene preview,
   **without the game running** and **without any service**. If a method only makes sense in a
   particular game state or after another call, that coupling belongs in the controller.

Structural consequences you get for free: `Game.Views` references only `CS.PF.Views`, so a View
*cannot* see a service or a controller — the compiler enforces what review would otherwise have to
catch.

## §4 — The three-tier init law

When something needs initialization it lands in **exactly one** of three tiers. This law is
**enforced by review** — the boot kernel cannot enforce it because, by design, **the kernel must
not know game features exist.**

**A thing becomes a boot node (tier 2) if and only if it must be _awaited_, can _fail
meaningfully_, or needs _external ordering_.** If none of the three hold, it is not a boot node.

| Tier | What it is | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| **1 — plain DI construction** | Constructed by the container, no boot node. | Synchronous, cannot meaningfully fail, needs no ordering. |
| **2 — a boot node (`IBootNode`)** | Declares `Requires`/`Provides` capabilities; the kernel schedules it. | Must be awaited, **or** can fail meaningfully, **or** needs external ordering. |
| **3 — `IAsyncStartable` in a child scope** | Feature-local async startup owned by a scene/feature scope, not the kernel. | Feature startup. A `MissionInit` node placed in the kernel is a **boundary violation**. |

**Race rule (holds across all tiers):** a node **ctor-injects only services whose readiness is
asserted by its `Requires` caps**. Injecting a service whose readiness your `Requires` does not
assert is precisely the race the boot graph exists to prevent.

Recipe: [`recipes/add-boot-node.md`](./recipes/add-boot-node.md).

## §5 — A SKU never edits framework code

Editing the framework from inside a consumer project is **always wrong**, and the reason differs by
mode:

- A package resolved from a registry or git lands in **`Library/PackageCache/…`**, which Unity
  **overwrites on every reimport/resolve**. Any edit there is **silently lost**.
- An edit to an **embedded** `Packages/com.classicspins.prototype-framework` in a SKU repo **forks
  the shared package**: the fix never reaches other SKUs and drifts from upstream forever.

To change framework code: **dev-link** a framework checkout (§5a), fix it **in the framework repo**,
run the framework's own gate (§5c), then bump the version your SKU pins.

### §5a — dev-link modes

The framework entry in your `Packages/manifest.json`:

| Mode | Manifest entry | When |
|---|---|---|
| **pinned** ⭐ | `"com.classicspins.prototype-framework": "0.1.0"` or a git `…#v0.1.0` tag | **CI / release — the clean default.** |
| **dev-link (`file:`)** | `"…": "file:../PrototypeFramework/Packages/com.classicspins.prototype-framework"` | **Daily co-dev** — edit the framework repo, see it live in the SKU. |
| **embedded** | *(no entry; physically under `Packages/`)* | A one-off local copy. |

**Edit that entry by hand** — it is one line in `Packages/manifest.json`. No framework tool writes it
and none reports which mode you are in; pick the mode yourself from the table above.

### §5b — the triage gate: "is this a local decision?"

| Change | Route |
|---|---|
| **A logic bug** — a wrong result, a leak, an off-by-one, **no boundary change** | Fix it in the framework repo via dev-link, gate it, release. A normal local decision. |
| **A spine change** — a new assembly, a new reference edge, a new RenderLayer, a new boot node, a new event type, or an edit to a shipped migrator | **Route to architecture review.** The spine is the shared invariant every SKU depends on. |

**If unsure, treat it as a spine change and route it.** An unnecessary review costs far less than an
unsanctioned spine edit shipped to every SKU.

### §5c — the framework runs its own gate BEFORE a version bump

In the **framework repo** (not your SKU):

```sh
cd HeadlessTests && dotnet test                             # the framework-pure ship gate
dotnet test SkuHeadlessTests                                # the sample-SKU gate — a SEPARATE CI step
sh Tools/CI/greps.sh source                                 # input-poll / lifecycle / MessagePipe-reg greps
dotnet run --project Packages/com.classicspins.prototype-framework/Tools~/Codegen/ScaffoldCli -- --check    # four-legs manifest↔scene↔Addressables↔class drift
```

All four green **before** the `package.json` version bump and tag. **Never bump-then-fix** — a red
bump ships the breakage to every SKU that pins the new version.

A green `HeadlessTests` says **nothing** about `SkuHeadlessTests` — they are separate projects and
separate CI steps, so a framework fix that breaks the sample SKU passes the first and fails CI.

**If your change adds a public framework type, run `pf-build.sh agentdocs` and commit both regenerated
`framework-api.index.json` files before the ship gate.** `AgentDocsSyncTests` lives *inside*
`dotnet test`, so a stale pack reddens gate 1 with a failure that looks unrelated to your change.

### §5d — cross-repo work tracking

Entries in `_bmad-output/implementation-artifacts/deferred-work.md` end with an `Owner:` tag in one
of exactly two buckets (keep the descriptive suffix):

- **`Owner: framework/*`** — belongs upstream (e.g. `framework/kernel-boot`). Fixed in the framework
  repo, flows back to every SKU.
- **`Owner: SKU/*`** — stays local to one game (e.g. `SKU/screen-pattern`), never touches framework
  code.

A `framework/*` item that turns out to need a spine change is routed per §5b before it is worked.

## §6 — What counts as a spine change

Memorize this list. Each item is an architecture decision, not a patch:

1. A **new assembly** — beyond the eight the SKU spine already declares. Creating those eight is
   *not* a spine change: `Framework/Setup Wizard` emits them, and adding an `.asmref` that joins a
   feature folder to one of them is ordinary work.
2. A **new reference edge** between assemblies (`AssemblyGraphTests` pins the graph by set-equality,
   so both a missing and an extra edge redden CI by name). **Widening `Game.Presentation` back to
   VContainer is this**, not a convenience: that tier deliberately names no container type, exactly
   like `CS.PF.Presentation`.
3. A **new RenderLayer** (rule #7 — must pass the three-condition test in `architecture-map.md` §5).
4. A **new boot node** in the kernel (a feature-local one is tier 3, §4 — that is not a spine
   change).
5. A **new event type** (each requires an explicit `RegisterMessageBroker<T>` in an installer;
   MessagePipe has no source generator).
6. An **edit to a shipped migrator** (rule #2 — append instead).

---

## §7 — Package requirements

- **The OpenUPM scoped registry is mandatory.** A UPM `package.json` cannot declare git
  dependencies, so VContainer, UniTask, MessagePipe, and LitMotion resolve through an **OpenUPM
  scoped registry** that every consuming `Packages/manifest.json` must configure. A consumer missing
  it gets a resolution error naming the missing scope — **that is the intended failure mode, not a
  bug.** The block to add is in the package `README.md`.
- **All version pins are minimums — never downgrade.** Older VContainer/UniTask/MessagePipe break on
  Unity 6.2+ editor API removals.
- **The framework name `PrototypeFramework` is permanent** — there is no graduation rename. `CS.PF.*`
  is prose-only shorthand; **namespace ≡ assembly name, always.** In a SKU that is now enforced
  rather than hoped for: every `.cs` declares the namespace of the assembly its nearest ancestor
  `.asmdef`/`.asmref` puts it in, so a `using` line tells you which assembly — and therefore which
  dependencies — are in play. A file that says `namespace Game.Application` while sitting under a
  `Presentation/` folder is a defect even though it compiles.

## §8 — Commands available in a SKU

| Command | What it gates |
|---|---|
| `Framework/Doctor` (editor menu) | Registry, dep min-versions, config resolution, settings-in-scene, render rig, boot graph, `ConfigDefaults` registration, **agent-docs freshness**, and **check 15: the eight `.asmdef` anchors exist and every `.asmref` resolves** — the only local surface that catches a script silently falling into `Assembly-CSharp`. |
| `Framework/Setup Wizard` (editor menu) | First-run composition — including a sync of this pack, so a freshly composed SKU starts with the rules of the version it resolved, and the **assembly-spine emit** (the eight `.asmdef`s + their `IsExternalInit` shims). The spine emit is ungated, so an established SKU adopting it receives it too. It also writes a marker-delimited block into the repo-root `.gitattributes` (`*SDF.asset -diff` — TMP font atlases out of text diffs; lines outside the block are the SKU's and are never touched). |
| `Framework/Agent Docs/Sync` (editor menu) | Re-materialize this pack after a framework version bump. Works in every dev-link mode. |
| `Framework/Codegen/Generate` (editor menu) | Regenerate typed keys from the manifests. |
| `Framework/Scaffold/Sync` · `Framework/Scaffold/Check` | Create/verify scenes, dialogs, widgets, toasts from the manifests. |
| `Framework/Boot Graph` (editor menu) | Preview the scheduled boot order. |
| `Framework/Scope Debugger` (editor menu) | **PlayMode only.** The live `Root → Scene → Gameplay` scope tree, read from the container's own scopes, with the `IScopeTracker.Current` branch marked. Read-only. |

The engine-free suite needs **no** dev-link and no Unity — it is plain `dotnet`, and it is the command
§8a says to run every iteration:

```sh
sh Tools/pf/gate.sh                          # a SKU: greps + headless type-check + the FILTERED suite
cd HeadlessTests && dotnet test              # the framework's own engine-free project — seconds
```

A SKU's engine-free suite carries tests tagged `Slow` — a sweep, a soak, a fuzz — that its gate
filters out (`DEFAULT_TEST_FILTER="TestCategory!=Slow"`). Run the gate, not the bare command, and cap
anything whose termination you are unsure of with `Tools/pf/pf-timeout SECONDS COMMAND …` —
**`timeout(1)` does not exist on macOS**, and the recovery from `command not found` is usually to
re-run it uncapped, which is where the cost is.

Command-line equivalents (available when a framework checkout is dev-linked). Every one of these is
engine-free `dotnet` — they run with the Editor open and are safe in any loop:

```sh
Tools/Build/pf-build.sh agentdocs --check    # agent-doc pack drift gate (0 ok · 1 drift · 2 error)
Tools/Build/pf-build.sh codegen --check      # typed-key drift gate
Tools/Build/pf-build.sh validate             # loc-CSV duplicate keys/locales + cross-locale format-args
```

The remaining surfaces — `test`, `content`, `player` — shell out to Unity in `-batchmode` and are
**CI-only**. An agent does not run them locally; §8a says why and what to run instead.

Every surface shares one exit-code contract: **`0` Ok · `1` Drift · `2` Error.**

**How often to run which is a contract, not a preference — see §8a.**

### §8a — Test cadence: engine-free in the loop, Unity only where it can run

There are **three** rungs, not two, only the first has no Unity in it, and **only the first two are
things you run in a loop at all**:

| Rung | What it is | How you run it locally | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Engine-free** | Plain .NET, no Unity at all — Domain/Application and any kernel slices a SKU pulls into a `dotnet` project | `sh Tools/pf/gate.sh` — the SKU's gate script, which passes the filter. **Never a bare `dotnet test <project>`**: it also runs the `Slow` sweeps the filter keeps out of the loop | **seconds** |
| **Unity EditMode** | Needs the Editor, but no play mode | `Tools/pf/pf-tests` — one synchronous run through MCP `script-execute`, against the Editor already open | seconds for the fast tier; the `[Category("Slow")]` tier only when the diff draws |
| **Unity PlayMode** | The PlayMode *suite* — needs the Editor *in play mode* | **you do not** — CI owns it | n/a locally |

Beside those three sit **two things that are neither a rung nor a suite**. Both are a *single observed
play-mode session*, both run no tests, and each answers a question no rung above can reach:

- the **boot smoke** — *does this thing still start?* Earned by a **bootstrap/wiring** change.
- the **visual check** — *does this actually look right on screen?* Earned by a change that **draws**,
  and taken with the Unity-MCP **screenshot** tools.

Both are defined below. Both are bounded by a budget you state **before** entering play mode, and both
carry the same hard limit: **play mode is for looking, never for iterating.** The set of things that
must never be driven from play mode — a sweep over hundreds of levels being the canonical one — has its
own section, and it is not negotiable.

### The local rule is absolute: never run Unity batchmode

**An agent never runs `pf-build.sh test`, `pf-build.sh content`, or `pf-build.sh player` locally.** Not
"prefer not to", not "unless the Editor is closed" — never. Two independent reasons, either one
sufficient:

1. **It cannot run while the Editor is open** — which, during dev, is always. The open project holds
   `Temp/UnityLockfile` and a second Unity in `-batchmode` aborts on that lock before a single test
   executes. (Closed-Editor batchmode does work; that is CI's situation, not a dev loop's. Do not read
   this as "the command is broken" and go looking for the window where it is not.)
2. **It lies when it fails.** `pf-build.sh test` deliberately ignores Unity's exit code and gates on
   the parsed NUnit XML. An aborted batchmode run writes **no** XML — so the gate reads the
   *previous* run's `test-results-<platform>.xml` and prints a green `result=Passed` describing a run
   that never happened. A green that proves nothing is worse than a red.

**The one local Unity door is EditMode through the Editor that is already open**: MCP `tests-run`
with `testMode: "EditMode"`, or better, its synchronous replacement `Tools/pf/pf-tests`. There is no
second Unity and no lock to lose. Never drive a suite with per-class MCP `tests-run` calls. pf-tests starts ONE synchronous `TestRunnerApi` run over any set of classes and
reads the verdict from a file, so it pays neither the unfocused Editor's ~8 s per call nor the
gateway's 300 s cap. Name the classes in the loop, and run `--auto` once as the stage receipt: that
is the fast tier, plus the `[Category("Slow")]` capture tier when the diff draws. The measurements
are in `pf-gates`.

**The PlayMode suite is never run locally, by any door** — not batchmode, not MCP `tests-run` with
`testMode: "PlayMode"`. Enter/exit plus startup, multiplied by a whole suite, is too slow to belong
anywhere near a dev loop, and CI already runs it.

**What *is* allowed, when earned and bounded, are the two observed sessions below** — the **boot smoke**
(one boot, no suite) and the **visual check** (a short, budgeted look at named screens, captured with
the MCP screenshot tools). Neither is the suite, neither runs a test, and neither may be reported as
one. Note what this splits: entering play mode to **look** at a UI change is now a duty, while running
the PlayMode **suite** stays CI's. The door that opened is the Editor's Play button under a budget —
not `tests-run`, and never batchmode.

**Batchmode belongs exclusively to CI.** That is not a workaround, it is the division of labour AD-14
already describes: *the tool is a convenience;* **CI is the guardrail**. A dev loop that never launches
Unity is safe **because** the pipeline's Unity step re-runs both rungs, and for no other reason.

**Which makes that step the load-bearing claim, so treat it as a claim and not a fact.** The ban is
absolute either way — an agent does not get to launch batchmode because CI looks doubtful — but what
you may *report* depends entirely on whether that step ran. Read the step (§8a's precondition below
tells you what to look for), and if you cannot confirm it ran, say the rungs are **unverified**. Never
translate "CI owns it" into "it is covered".

**`git worktree`, a second clone, or any other separate checkout is not the answer.** It sidesteps the
lock, and it is still forbidden: a Unity project pays a full `Library` import from scratch, which
costs more than the run it was meant to enable.

### The default, and what earns the middle rung

Run the engine-free suite on **every iteration**. It is the inner loop and the only rung that is
never earned — it just runs.

- **A change earns EditMode** when it touches **Editor-side** code — a menu item, an importer, a
  Doctor check, a scaffold or codegen tool. Run it through `Tools/pf/pf-tests`.
- **A change earns the boot smoke** when it touches **bootstrap/wiring** — a boot node, a DI
  registration, an asmdef, a scaffold manifest, a RenderLayer, an event route, a scene rig, the
  first-scene config. Take it **once**, when that change is complete. See the next section.
- **A change that draws earns the visual check** — a View, a prefab, scene content, a design token, a
  layout, a transition or animation: any UI/UX surface a player looks at. Enter play mode **once**,
  reach the states you named, capture them with `screenshot-game-view`, read the images, and attach
  them to what you hand back. Rule #17 lands here: *finished is the default* is not a claim you may
  make about a screen nobody looked at, and "engine-free green but still wrong on screen" is exactly
  the failure this catches. See "The visual check" below.
  **The PlayMode *suite* is still not run locally** — the visual check replaces the eyeball, not the
  suite, so a View's automated PlayMode fixtures remain CI's. Say which half is unproven.
- **Nothing is earned** for model/rules/parsing edits the engine-free suite already proves, for doc
  or comment edits, or for a refactor that suite covers end to end. "Just to be safe" is not a
  reason, and it is never a reason to boot.
- **Fits none of the above?** Run MCP EditMode and report the change as PlayMode-unproven. An
  unclassifiable change is not a licence to run nothing, and it is never a licence to run batchmode.
- **No engine-free project in this SKU?** Then MCP EditMode is the inner loop, and everything above
  about the PlayMode suite still holds.

### The boot smoke — one boot, not a suite

Wiring is the one class of change where every rung above is structurally blind. The engine-free suite
never constructs the container; EditMode never enters play mode; and the failure mode of a bad boot
node or a missing DI registration is not a wrong number — it is **nothing starts**, which no green
count anywhere will tell you. So one door stays open, deliberately narrow.

**Before you boot.** Three preconditions, each of which turns the smoke into a false green if skipped:

1. **`editor-application-get-state` first.** If the Editor is **already in play mode**, someone is
   using it: `isPlaying: true` is then a no-op you would mistake for a boot, and stopping it would end
   a session you did not start. Abort and say so.
2. **Every open scene saved, and the *right* scene open.** Play mode runs what is **in memory**, not
   what is on disk — a green boot over an unsaved rig describes a scene that does not exist in the
   commit. And a boot with the wrong scene open builds no container at all, which logs nothing and
   reads as clean.
3. **Compilation finished.** `editor-application-set-state` refuses while
   `EditorUtility.scriptCompilationFailed` is true and hands you the errors — but it does **not** wait
   for a compile still in flight. Refresh the AssetDatabase, let it settle, and check the returned
   snapshot is neither compiling nor importing. Booting stale assemblies proves the code you did not
   write.

**The door.** Unity-MCP against the Editor already open:

```
console-clear-logs                                # takes the human's console with it — say so
editor-application-set-state  { "isPlaying": true }
  … wait for the boot to reach a completion signal you can name …
console-get-logs                                  # explicit maxEntries — the default cap truncates
screenshot-game-view                              # only if the change draws
editor-application-set-state  { "isPlaying": false }
console-get-logs                                  # AGAIN — see below
```

**Never** MCP `tests-run` with `testMode: "PlayMode"`, and never batchmode: those run the suite, and
the suite is CI's. Leave the Editor as you found it — play mode exited.

**The two log reads are not redundancy.** Boot is asynchronous — awaited boot nodes, a first-scene
load, Addressables — so a read fired straight after `isPlaying: true` can return before the failure
exists. And **`[PoolLeak]` is emitted on scope *dispose***, i.e. after play mode exits, so a
single-read procedure structurally cannot see the one WARN rule #11 calls a bug.

**The pass criterion is not "no exceptions".** Two ways a naive read lies:

- **Warnings count.** Rule #11: a `[PoolLeak]` / "rented leak" WARN is a **bug to fix**, not noise. A
  boot exercising rent/return is exactly where one surfaces. Filter for errors *and* warnings.
- **Absence of errors is not evidence of a boot.** A boot node awaiting forever logs nothing and
  throws nothing. Require a **positive** completion signal — the boot report, the first scene actually
  up — within a bound you state. No signal inside that bound is a **red**, not a green.

**When.** At the point the wiring change is **complete**, not between edits. The smoke is a
verification act, not a build step. Loop on the engine-free suite; boot at the end.

**The ceiling — ten entries into play mode in one dev turn.** *One dev turn* = one unit of work you
hand back to a human — a story, a task, one response. **One boot covers every wiring change completed
in that turn**, not one boot per change; the headroom above that is for re-entering after a fix, not
for booting change by change. **An eleventh entry in one dev turn means you are using play mode as a
loop — stop and go back down a rung.** No counter enforces this; it is here so you can notice yourself
crossing it. The ceiling is shared with the visual check below and counts **entries into play mode**,
not reasons for them: one session can serve as both.

**What it proves.** That the app booted and the log is clean. Nothing else. It is **not** a PlayMode
test pass — it proves the app started, **never that a suite passed** — and reporting it as one is the
failure the next section exists to prevent. Report it on its own line: *"boot smoke clean (MCP, 1
boot); PlayMode suite not run — CI-owned, unverified."*

**When it is red.** Fix the cause, then re-boot to confirm — a confirm boot is well inside the
ceiling. **Three reds on the same cause and you stop booting**: name the failure and hand it over
rather than re-entering to re-read a failure you already have. That is the exit, and it is why the two
rules do not deadlock. A red you have not investigated is never handed to CI as "unverified" — you
already have the evidence that something is broken. A red traceable to something the change never
touched is **pre-existing**: name it in the report, do not silently repair unrelated breakage.

**When two lists both fire, the earn wins** — the same tie-break the EditMode rung uses. A refactor
the engine-free suite covers that also moves a DI registration earns the boot smoke. A change that is
both Editor-side and wiring earns **both**: EditMode first, then the boot.

**Unearned play mode is still banned.** Not by MCP, not by pressing Play in the Editor to eyeball
something. The allowance is one boot for a wiring change, not a licence to watch the game run.

**When the door is shut.** Three ways, one answer — and it shuts the visual check with it, since
both sessions use the same door. Compilation is failing — fix that first, do not retry blindly. The
Editor is unfocused on macOS — Unity-MCP does not fail cleanly here, it **stalls**, so do not sit
waiting on it. Or the SKU has no Unity-MCP at all — then this door does not exist for you. In every
case: **no batchmode fallback.** Ask the human to focus the Editor if one is there; otherwise name the
session you could not take — boot smoke, visual check, or both — hand it to CI, and finish.

One caveat specific to an unattended session — and it has **one project setting behind it**. With
*Run In Background* off, the Editor's player loop only advances while the window is focused and
repainting: an unfocused play mode sits at `Time.frameCount == 1` forever, every PlayerLoop-driven
`await` in boot hangs to its node's hard timeout, and nothing is ever drawn to screenshot. **Check that
setting before concluding the door is shut** — `runInBackground: 1` in
`ProjectSettings/ProjectSettings.asset` (*Project Settings ▸ Player ▸ Resolution and Presentation ▸ Run
In Background*, i.e. `PlayerSettings.runInBackground`). The **Setup Wizard's compose turns it on** (phase
B, beside the physics scale), so a freshly composed SKU is already right; a project composed before that
step, or one that turned it back off, is the case to fix rather than to give up on. What Run In
Background does **not** fix is Unity-MCP's own macOS focus stall: if the MCP call itself never returns,
the door is shut regardless of the setting. A genuinely shut door is **not a red** — do not file the
resulting timeouts as product bugs, and do not report an unfocused session's blank capture as a visual
check.

### The visual check — screenshots of named states, never a sweep

Rule #17 makes *finished* the default and §3's View tests make a View logic-free — together they mean
the only place a UI/UX change is genuinely proven is **on screen**. The engine-free suite cannot draw.
EditMode never enters play mode. Even a PlayMode fixture asserts numbers, not appearance. So a change
that draws earns one **observed, budgeted** play session whose output is **images you look at**.

**Write the budget down before you enter.** Two things, in the report or the story's verification
section, *before* the first `isPlaying: true`:

1. **The states you will capture, by name** — "the board at level 1", "the level-complete dialog", "the
   empty state", "the error panel". A list you can finish.
2. **A wall-clock ceiling for the session**, and what you do on hitting it: exit play mode, report what
   you captured, and name what you did not reach.

A session you cannot describe in advance is the sweep the next section forbids, wearing another name.

**The door** — Unity-MCP against the Editor already open; the boot smoke's sequence plus captures:

```
console-clear-logs                                # takes the human's console with it — say so
editor-application-set-state  { "isPlaying": true }
  … reach each named state — drive it with script-execute / gameobject-* if it needs input …
screenshot-game-view                              # once per named state — these images ARE the output
  … screenshot-camera for one camera; screenshot-isolated for one object on a clean ground …
console-get-logs                                  # explicit maxEntries — the default cap truncates
editor-application-set-state  { "isPlaying": false }
console-get-logs                                  # AGAIN — [PoolLeak] is emitted on scope dispose
```

**Capture at FHD, in the project's own orientation** — `1080×1920` on a portrait rig, `1920×1080` on a
landscape one. Read which off the rig's design rect (`WorldSpaceCanvasScaler.ReferenceResolution`, the
host's `CanvasCameraFitter._referenceResolution`); never hardcode the other orientation, and never let a
tool pick for you. It matters most for `screenshot-camera`, which defaults to landscape FHD **and swaps
that aspect onto the camera**: on a portrait rig an unsized capture shows an aspect the game never
ships, and the mutated aspect then corrupts every later capture in the same session.

**Never** MCP `tests-run` with `testMode: "PlayMode"`, and never batchmode: those run the suite, and the
suite is CI's. Leave play mode exited.

**The boot smoke's three preconditions apply unchanged**, for the same reasons — not already in play
mode, every scene saved with the right one open, compilation finished. A screenshot of an unsaved rig
describes a scene that is not in the commit, which is worse than no screenshot.

**Capturing is not verifying — the reading is.** Check each image against `pf-visual-design`'s
finished-surface checklist and the artist spec if one exists: a deliberate ground rather than the rig's
default, drawn empty states, one spacing rhythm, a type hierarchy, nothing clipped at the safe rect,
nothing overlapping, legible at device size. Then **write what you saw**. A screenshot attached with no
written reading is a file, not evidence.

**And the log still counts.** The same two reads bracket the session, and the same pass criterion holds:
warnings count, `[PoolLeak]` is a bug, and a screen that renders over a console full of errors is a red.

### What play mode must never be used for

**Play mode is for looking, never for iterating.** Both observed sessions are a single sitting with a
stated end. Anything whose running time is a function of a content set, a search, or a clock does **not**
belong in play mode locally — no matter how tempting the door is now that it is open:

- **Sweeping a content set** — playing every level in the catalogue, every item in a palette, every row
  of a table. **Hundreds of levels is the canonical forbidden case.**
- **Solver, exhaustive or combinatorial runs** — proving N levels are all solvable, or that every
  permutation of a rule holds.
- **Soak, perf, or long timed simulation** — "leave it running and see"; anything measured in minutes.
- **Anything with no bound you can state in advance.** If you cannot say when it stops *before* you
  start it, it is a sweep.

These are not merely slow — play mode gives them a **false home**. They are data-and-rules questions,
which is exactly what the **engine-free** rung answers in seconds, deterministically, with a failure
message naming the offending case. A play-mode sweep answers the same question with a frozen Editor, a
human locked out of their own session, and no artefact at the end. Anything that genuinely needs the
engine at that scale is **CI's**.

**Sample, never sweep.** Where visual confidence over a large set is the real goal, capture a **named
handful** — the first, the last, and the extremes the spec calls out — and say in the report that it is
a sample and which members it covers. Three named levels with screenshots is evidence. "I played
through them" is not.

**The ceiling, and the two sessions together.** **Ten entries into play mode in one dev turn** — one
dev turn being one unit of work handed back to a human. **One play session covers every change completed
in that turn**: a turn that touches both wiring and a View takes **one** session serving as boot smoke
*and* visual check, never two, and the headroom above that is for re-entering after a fix. **An eleventh
entry in one dev turn means you are using it as a loop — stop, drop a rung, and report what you have.**
Red? Fix it and re-enter to confirm; three reds on the same cause are named and handed over, not chased
with a fourth.

**What it proves.** What was on screen, in the states you captured, in the Editor, on this machine's
aspect ratio. Nothing about the states you did not capture, nothing about a device, and — exactly like
the boot smoke — **never that a suite passed**. Report it on its own line.

### What an EditMode-only loop actually covers — and does not

**Know the size of the hole before you rely on the rung.** EditMode covers only fixtures in a test
assembly that declares `"includePlatforms": ["Editor"]`. Everything in an assembly with
`"includePlatforms": []` is PlayMode **in full** and an EditMode run does not touch it.

*(Shape, this repo — a consuming SKU has its own and must look.* The only EditMode-classified assembly
is the framework's `Tests/Editor`, and it holds Editor **tooling** fixtures: menu items, importers,
Doctor checks, the scaffold and codegen tools. The framework's `Tests/Runtime` and the sample SKU's
`Game.Tests` are both `"includePlatforms": []`, hence PlayMode in full. So framework runtime and SKU
Views have **zero** local coverage here.*)*

**Do not quote a test count you did not just observe.** Attribute counts under-report — one
`[TestCase]` or `[TestCaseSource]` is many cases — and nothing in the pack pins these numbers to the
asmdefs, so any figure written here rots the next time a fixture lands. Count at the moment you report,
or describe the shape and skip the number.

So: **an EditMode pass is never evidence about runtime.** Reporting one as though it were is the
specific failure this section exists to prevent.

### Why MCP EditMode is cheaper — stated accurately

Not because it skips a domain reload. `tests-run` refreshes the AssetDatabase first and, if scripts
changed, persists the run and resumes it **after** the reload — you pay that reload either way. What
it avoids is the **Editor boot and the project import** that a fresh `-batchmode -nographics` Editor
pays before the first test executes — comparing EditMode to EditMode, neither side enters play mode. That is the order-of-magnitude
difference, and it is structural, not a tuning artefact.

Two preconditions come with that door, and both fail loudly rather than silently:

- **Every open scene must be saved.** A dirty scene aborts the run with an
  `InvalidOperationException` listing them.
- **On macOS the Unity window must be focused**, or Unity-MCP returns null and the call stalls. MCP
  is a **human-attended** door by construction — which is exactly why it is never the scripted or CI
  leg.

**So the earned EditMode rung can be unavailable, and that case has an answer.** If MCP returns null
(no Editor, or an unfocused one — an unattended session is the normal way this happens), or aborts on
dirty scenes, **do not fall back to batchmode.** Ask the human to focus or save if one is there;
otherwise treat the rung exactly like the PlayMode suite — say which rung you could not run and why,
hand it to CI, and finish. The ban has no fallback arm, by design: there is no state of the world in
which batchmode is the answer locally. The same holds for an earned boot smoke: an unfocused Editor
means no boot, not a batchmode one.

### Say what you skipped, out loud

*"engine-free suite green (1548); EditMode not run — no Editor-side change; boot smoke clean (MCP, 1
boot); visual check: 3 states captured (board L1, level-complete dialog, empty state) — screenshots
attached, read against the checklist; PlayMode suite not run locally — CI owns it, unverified"* is the
shape. Report the count for what you actually ran, and never phrase a partial run so a reader would
assume the whole suite ran. **The boot smoke and the visual check each get their own clause, never
folded into the suite's** — "PlayMode checked" would be a false claim about a suite you did not run.
**A visual check with no images is not a visual check**: name the states and attach the captures, or
report it as not taken.

**Do not assume the EditMode rung is green just because you ran it.** Two things bite here. Its
outcome is not a constant: in this repo the last recorded batchmode EditMode run was **red** (two
`BuildEntryEditorTests` failures, owner `framework/build-entry-appid-test`). And MCP EditMode is not
result-equivalent to CI's — those two failures are documented as batchmode-specific (no
`FrameworkSettings` asset resolved, ambient `PlayerSettings`), so **green under MCP and red in CI are
both expected outcomes of the same code**. Report which door you used.

**And do not overstate CI either.** You did not watch CI run. Report the Unity rungs as **CI-owned
and unverified** — naming them as covered is a claim you have no evidence for.

**Where to say it.** In whatever you hand back for this unit of work — the report, the story's
verification section, the PR body. Somewhere a reviewer reads before accepting it.

**Ending a story.** Engine-free → the drift gates → MCP EditMode if it was earned → the one play
session if it was earned, last and once — serving as boot smoke, visual check, or both. That is the whole local sequence; there is no final batchmode pass to
schedule. If an earned run comes back red, fix it and **re-run that rung once** before calling anything
green — a fix made after a red run is unverified until the rung says otherwise. (A local working order,
not CI's: CI runs the drift gates at step 3, Unity at step 4, the headless suite at step 5.)

### The precondition, and how to check it (AD-14)

Skipping the Unity rungs locally is safe **only** because CI re-runs them. **Check, do not assume**,
and check the *gate*, not just the *file*: grep the workflows for `--platform PlayMode`, then look at
whether that step is unconditional. Three outcomes:

- **(a)** a leg that runs **and blocks the merge** ⇒ everything above applies as written.
- **(b)** a leg that is advisory (`continue-on-error: true`), narrowed by an `if:`, branch-filtered,
  skipped on forks — **or declared in a repo with no remote to run it** ⇒ that **counts as no
  PlayMode leg**. A failure nobody is stopped by is not a gate, and a workflow nothing executes is
  not a pipeline.
- **(c)** no PlayMode leg, or no CI at all ⇒ nothing is gating that suite. The local ban still
  stands — an agent does not get to launch batchmode because CI is missing — so **name the missing
  leg** in your report and escalate it to the human. An ungated suite is a decision for a human to
  make, not a hole for an agent to quietly paper over. **The visual check narrows this hole but does
  not close it:** in a SKU with no CI, the screenshots are the *only* runtime evidence that exists, so
  take them and read them properly — and still say plainly that the automated PlayMode suite is
  ungated. Images of three screens are not a suite, and reporting them as one is the same false claim
  in a new costume.

**And note a fourth outcome the three above do not cover: a leg that is declared, unconditional, and
merge-blocking, yet has never been observed to succeed.** That is this repo today. `ci.yml` step 4
declares both rungs unconditionally (pinned by `CadenceCiLegTests`), but `docs/m5-pilot-acceptance.md`
marks that step **DEFERRED**, no PlayMode results artifact has ever existed, and `deferred-work.md`
(`Owner: framework/playmode-batchmode-stall`) records that batchmode PlayMode **stalls indefinitely
with no results XML**. A declaration is not an execution: `CadenceCiLegTests` proves the leg is
*declared*, never that it *ran*. Report accordingly — **CI-owned, unverified** — and do not present
declaration as coverage.

**An empty run is not a green run.** Because of the trap below, an EditMode rung can report **0
tests** — every fixture having been classified PlayMode. Zero tests executed is not evidence; say so
rather than banking it.

**When two rules both fire, the earn-it rule wins.** A doc-comment edit *inside an Editor tool* is
still an Editor-side change: earn beats "earns nothing".

### The empty-`includePlatforms` trap

A test asmdef with `"includePlatforms": []` is classified PlayMode **in full**. The EditMode runner
then finds *nothing* in it, so every fixture — including pure arithmetic that never touches the
engine — is stranded behind a rung nobody runs locally. The remedy is a sibling test assembly with
`"includePlatforms": ["Editor"]` holding the engine-light fixtures. The framework constrains neither
that field nor a SKU's assembly count, so the remedy is open to any SKU — but where a SKU's own spine
pins its assembly set or its asmdef fields, adding the sibling is a **routed spine change** (§6), not
a local edit. **The pack ships this trap in its own exemplars:** the framework's `Tests/Runtime`
asmdef and the sample SKU's test asmdef both declare `"includePlatforms": []`. The framework's
`Tests/Editor` asmdef is the remedy already applied — `"includePlatforms": ["Editor"]` — and it is
what gives the EditMode rung anything to run here.

### Two mechanics worth knowing even though CI owns them

**Trust the XML, not the exit code.** Batchmode `-runTests` exit codes are unreliable, so
`pf-build.sh test` gates on the parsed NUnit XML (`--results`) and fails on any failed or errored
test and on absent or malformed XML. Read this as background for reading a CI log, not as an
invitation to run the command.

**All three batchmode surfaces refuse to run against an open project.** `test`, `content` and `player`
check `Temp/UnityLockfile` and exit `2` naming it rather than launching a Unity that would abort. `test`
additionally moves any previous results XML aside to `<results>.prev` before launching, so an aborted
run can never be mistaken for a passing one and no evidence is destroyed. If you see that exit 2 the
tool is telling you to use MCP `tests-run` or leave it to CI — **not** to close the human's Editor.

One case deserves its own line: Unity leaves that lockfile behind when it is **killed or hangs on
exit**, so the file can outlive every Editor. An orphaned lock would otherwise brick all three surfaces
permanently, CI included — hence `PF_ALLOW_LOCKED=1`, correct **only** once you have confirmed no Editor
is running. It is not a way around the ban.

**A sibling MCP skill scopes its advice differently.** The Unity-MCP `tests-run` tool documents
"EditMode is faster; prefer it during iteration" — true *within Unity*, and still not the rule here:
the engine-free rung sits **below** both Unity rungs and is the inner loop.

**If your repo already hand-wrote a cadence policy** outside the `PF:AGENT-DOCS` markers, **reduce it
to the SKU-specific facts** once this section syncs in — which suites actually exist here, what they
are named, which of them is all-PlayMode and why, the local deferral tracking that. Delete the parts
this section now owns (the default, the earn-it rules, the local ban, the precondition, the trap).
The sync cannot touch anything outside its markers, so whatever you keep will never be updated for
you, and any duplicated rule will drift from this one.
